predecessors.name: Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal (Grand Principality of Vladimir)
predecessors.text: Moscow, 'the least valuable' of Alexander Nevsky's patrimonies that his youngest son Daniel received in 1263

successors.name: Tsardom of Russia
successors.text: the whole realm of the grand princes of Moscow, 'crowned as the first Russian tsar in 1547, thereby formally establishing the Tsardom of Russia'

ledger.x: 1263: Daniel receives Moscow, the seed of the Muscovite principality.
ledger.cpn: Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal (Grand Principality of Vladimir)

ledger.x: 1301: Daniel defeats Ryazan and takes Kolomna and Serpukhov.
1302: Ivan of Pereslavl bequeaths his lands to Daniel.
ledger.cpn: Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal (Grand Principality of Vladimir)

ledger.x: 1304: Daniel's sons seize Mozhaysk from Smolensk.

1305: Dmitrov, Klin and the rest of Cliopatria's 1305 step, 107 cells at 35.9-39.3 E, 54.8-57.3 N beyond Daniel's core, the 30 km discs at Kolomna and Serpukhov (1301) and the 35 km disc at Pereslavl-Zalessky (1302).
ledger.cpn: Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal (Grand Principality of Vladimir)

ledger.x: 1333: 18 cells north of Moscow in the Uglich and Mologa country pass from Vladimir-Suzdal.
ledger.cpn: Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal (Grand Principality of Vladimir)

ledger.x: 1344: Moscow takes over Beloozero.
1344: Galich, Kostroma and the Vologda country pass from Vladimir-Suzdal, the lands credited to Ivan I's purchases (Galich) or to Dmitry's incorporation of 'Beloozero, Galich and Uglich'.
ledger.cpn: Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal (Grand Principality of Vladimir)

ledger.x: 1344: 68 cells in the Volga-Mologa country south-east of Novgorod pass to Moscow; the Novgorod dossier has the same loss.
1344: the remaining 49 cells of the 1344 step were in no Cliopatria shape; no page opened describes them.
1363: 14 cells on the Smolensk border south-west of Moscow.
1368: Moscow's army invades Tver.
1375: 37 cells (Yuryev-Polsky and its neighbours) pass from Vladimir-Suzdal; the Vladimir-Suzdal dossier says its page names Yuriev-Polsky and dates nothing.
ledger.cpn: Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal (Grand Principality of Vladimir)

ledger.x: 1 September 1375: Tver makes peace.
19 May 1389: Vasily I takes the throne of Vladimir together with Moscow.
ledger.cpn: Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal (Grand Principality of Vladimir)

ledger.x: 1392: Vasily I takes Nizhny Novgorod and the Suzdal lands.
1397: Moscow annexes the Dvina Lands.
1398: the Dvina Lands go back to Novgorod.
1397-1398: Vologda, Veliky Ustyug and the Komi lands are annexed.
1398: Kaluga and the Oka country join Moscow.
1415: 29 cells at Bezhetsk, which the Vladimir-Suzdal shape holds, pass to Moscow.
1444-1445: Ulugh Muhammad occupies Nizhny Novgorod.
1445: the occupation ends.
1452: Vasily II presents Gorodets Meshchersky to Qasim, who founds the Qasim Khanate in Moscow's sphere.
1463: Moscow absorbs the Principality of Yaroslavl.

1463: 96 more cells of the 1463 step (37.9-41.9 E, 57.2-59.2 N, north of Yaroslavl round Rybinsk and the Mologa) come from Cliopatria's Vladimir-Suzdal shape of 1453, beyond the 50 km disc at Yaroslavl and the Rostov disc.
ledger.cpn: Principality of Vladimir-Suzdal (Grand Principality of Vladimir)

ledger.x: 1463: 125 cells on the Vologda side pass from Novgorod; the Novgorod dossier says no page dates it.
1468: Ibrahim of Kazan overruns Vyatka in answer to the Russian raid on Kazan's Vyatka region, in the 1467-1469 war in which Ivan III did not get his candidate on the throne.
Autumn 1469: Kholmsky besieges Kazan and the 1469 peace recognizes Ibrahim.
July 1471: Ivan III and Novgorod fight on the Shelon.
July 1471: Novgorod becomes a protectorate of Moscow.
July 1471: the Shelon is won and the Treaty of Korostyn follows; Ivan III executed Dmitry Boretsky on 24 July 1471.
1474: Moscow absorbs Rostov.
January 1478: Ivan III annexes Novgorod.
January 1478: the Novgorod protectorate ends in annexation (see the gain above).
1482: the Uglich country enters Moscow's shape.
1482: 84 more cells (29.9-37.6 E, 57.9-61.6 N) enter the shape that neither the Novgorod 1475 nor the Tver 1486 shape holds; no page opened dates or names them.
1485: Ivan III marches on Tver.
12 September 1485: Ivan III's forces seize Tver.
12 September 1485: Ivan III annexes Tver.
9 June 1487: Moscow takes Kazan.
July 1487: the occupation turns into vassalage.
1487: Kazan becomes Moscow's vassal.
1489: Moscow takes the Vyatka land.
August 1492: Ivan III invades Lithuania.
5 February 1494: the 'eternal' peace gives Moscow Vyazma and the upper Oka.
5 February 1494: the first Muscovite-Lithuanian war ends in the 'eternal' peace.
July 1500: the second war.
1502: 22 cells on the Arctic coast (48-50 E, 69 N) join Moscow.
25 March 1503: the second Muscovite-Lithuanian war ends in a six-year truce.
25 March 1503: the six-year truce gives Moscow Chernigov, Novgorod-Seversk and Starodub.
March 1503: Gomel is Muscovite when the war of 1500-1503 ends.
1503: 152 further cells of the Seversk step were in no Cliopatria shape (steppe and forest between Lithuania and the Horde); no page describes them.
1503: the Seversk lands pass to Moscow with their own princes.
1503: Starodub passes to Moscow with its own princes; see the Novgorod-Seversk event above for the reading (vassal land until the annexation of 1523, confidence 1).
1505: Kazan breaks away.
January 1510: Moscow annexes Pskov.
1512: 120 cells in the south (34.6-38.1 E, 50.9-53.1 N) enter the shape that neither the 1507 shape nor Pskov's holds; no page opened dates or names them.
December 1512: Moscow invades Lithuania a fourth time ('Moscow invaded in December 1512'); the sieges of Smolensk in 1513 failed.
31 July - 1 August 1514: Smolensk surrenders to Vasili III.
1516: 42 cells on the Lithuanian side (29.3-31.7 E, 55.7-56.9 N) leave Moscow's shape; no page opened dates a loss there.
1519: 94 cells at 28-32 E, 54-57 N pass from Lithuania in the shape.

1519: 22 cells (30.6-31.5 E, 52.5-56.0 N) leave Moscow's shape while 94 are added; the war page has Moscow beating Lithuanian forces at Polotsk in 1518 and invading Lithuania again in 1519 ('raiding Orsha, Mogilev, Minsk, Vitebsk, and Polotsk') and no cession.
1521: Moscow annexes Ryazan.
1522: the fourth war ends in a five-year truce 'for Russia to retain control of Smolensk'; it was later extended to 1534.
1522: Novgorod-Seversk is annexed.
1522: Novgorod-Seversk joins Moscow's own land.
1523: Starodub is annexed.
1523: Starodub joins Moscow's own land (see the vassal_end above).
1534: the fifth war.
1535: Lithuanian and Polish forces retake Gomel.
1537: 'Lithuania and Russia negotiated a five-year truce, without prisoner exchange'; the page gives no exact date.
1547: the grand prince is crowned tsar and the realm becomes the Tsardom of Russia.

wars.name: Daniel's war with Ryazan
wars.outcome: Moscow victory: Kolomna and Serpukhov incorporated.

wars.name: Moscow-Tver conflict under Dmitry Donskoy
wars.outcome: Moscow's army invaded Tver by 1368 and again in 1370; the treaty of 1 September 1375 made Mikhail of Tver acknowledge Dmitry as his 'elder brother'.

wars.name: Battle of Skornishchevo
wars.outcome: Moscow defeated Ryazan at Skornishchevo on 14 December 1371; no border change.

wars.name: Moscow against Mamai (Vozha 1378, Kulikovo 1380)
wars.outcome: Dmitry stopped paying tribute to Mamai from 1374, beat a Mongol army on the Vozha in 1378 and won at Kulikovo in 1380.

wars.name: Tokhtamysh's sack of Moscow
wars.outcome: Tokhtamysh sacked Moscow; Dmitry pledged loyalty to him and was reinstated as grand prince of Vladimir.

wars.name: Vasily I and Vytautas
wars.outcome: They 'waged war against each other in 1406-1408'; Vytautas attacked Novgorod and Pskov.

wars.name: Edigu's raid on Moscow
wars.outcome: Edigu burned Nizhny Novgorod, Gorodets and Rostov and 'failed to take Moscow, though he had still burnt it'; Vasily resumed submission to the Horde in 1412.

wars.name: Muscovite war of succession (Vasily II and the Galich line)
wars.outcome: Yury 'claimed the throne again in 1431 with the support of the population of Galich'; Vasily II accepted Kolomna as an appanage in 1433; 'Galich was captured by Vasily in 1450'.

wars.name: Ulugh Muhammad's wars with Moscow (Belyov 1437, Nizhny Novgorod 1444-1445, Suzdal 1445)
wars.outcome: Ulugh Muhammad defeated Muscovite troops at Belyov (1437), occupied Nizhny Novgorod in 1444-1445 and won the Battle of Suzdal (7 July 1445), where Vasily II was captured and later ransomed.

wars.name: Kazan succession war and Vyatka (1467-1469)
wars.outcome: Ivan III did not get his candidate on the throne; the 1469 peace recognized Ibrahim.

wars.name: Muscovite-Novgorodian war of 1471 (Shelon)
wars.outcome: Moscow won on the Shelon on 14 July 1471; the Treaty of Korostyn made Novgorod 'a patrimony of the grand prince' with its autonomy kept.

wars.name: Annexation of Novgorod
wars.outcome: Ivan III sent armies against the city in winter 1477-1478 and took direct control in January 1478.

wars.name: Great Stand on the Ugra River
wars.outcome: The Horde's Ahmed retreated into the steppe on 11 November 1480; traditionally the end of the 'Tatar yoke'.

wars.name: Annexation of Tver (1485)
wars.outcome: Ivan III's forces seized Tver on 12 September 1485 and Tver was formally annexed; its last prince fled to Lithuania.

wars.name: Moscow's capture of Kazan (1486-1487)
wars.outcome: Muscovy won: the siege began on 18 May 1487, Kazan fell on 9 June 1487 and Moxammat Amin was installed; the Ivan III page makes Kazan a vassal state.

wars.name: Muscovite-Lithuanian War (1492-1494)
wars.outcome: Peace of 5 February 1494: Lithuania loses the Principality of Vyazma and the upper Oka (about 87,000 km2).

wars.name: Muscovite-Lithuanian War (1500-1503)
wars.outcome: Six-year truce of 25 March 1503: Lithuania loses Chernigov, Novgorod-Seversk, Starodub and the upper Oka (about 210,000 km2, a third of its land).

wars.name: Kazan revolt and war of 1505-1507
wars.outcome: Kazan won: Moxammat Amin asserted independence from Moscow in 1505, defeated the Russians on 25 June 1506, then sued for peace and paid homage to Vasily III.

wars.name: Muscovite-Lithuanian War (1507-1508)
wars.outcome: Eternal peace of 8 October 1508 'maintained the territorial accords of the 1503 truce'.

wars.name: Muscovite-Lithuanian War (1512-1522)
wars.outcome: Smolensk fell in July 1514; Lithuania won at Orsha on 8 September 1514 and Moscow at Polotsk in 1518; the 1522 truce let Russia 'retain control of Smolensk' (about 56,000 km2).

wars.name: Crimean and Kazan campaigns of Vasili III
wars.outcome: Defeat on the Oka and tribute in 1519; a 1521 Crimean invasion left Vasili bound as a vassal; Islam I Giray repelled in 1527; Kazan campaigns of 1523 and 1524 and the pretender Cangali set on Kazan's throne in 1531-1532.

wars.name: Muscovite-Lithuanian War (1534-1537)
wars.outcome: Moscow kept Sebezh and Zavoloche; Lithuania took Gomel and Starodub; five-year truce, no exchange of prisoners (the page's table, which shows a Lithuanian gain of 20,000 km2, conflicts with its text).

certainty.note: The frontiers of the Moscow lands are approximate throughout: the pages give towns and principalities, not lines.

The Lithuanian frontier is settled by treaties in 1494, 1503, 1508 and 1522, but the pages list towns and districts, not a boundary, so it stays soft; the northern and eastern dominions (Pomorye, Pechora, Vyatka) are soft throughout.
